label: adult-s4
summary: The model predicts the chance of a low income (the lower of the two income classes in the data) as a sigmoid of a sum of parts; on the training split its AUC is 0.9099 and its mean predicted chance 75.7% against an observed rate of 76.1%. The household terms matter most (switching them off takes the AUC to 0.8465): wives and husbands married to a civilian spouse get the lowest predicted chance and people living as a child of the household the highest. More education lowers the predicted chance at each step from 11th grade (84% for the typical case) to a doctorate (14%), and capital gains lower it steeply (31% at 5000 US dollars, against 71% at none). Age acts as a U: the predicted chance falls from 88% at 20 years to 52% at 50 years, where a hidden hinge opens, and rises to 82% at 80 years. Other service, clerical, handler and manual or farm jobs, a missing occupation and birth outside the United States raise the predicted chance by fixed steps; longer hours and executive work lower it. Two hidden regimes are fitted to small groups: birth in Colombia (64 training rows) opens the age hinge so far that the predicted chance is close to certain, and birth in Portugal (49 rows) lowers the score by a large step that their observed rate (81.6%) does not support. The hidden chain through wife, India and unmarried reaches the output on 0 training rows, so relationships act through their direct edges.
